paras: The threatened lynching and banishment of Doe Moran took place in Stanford, Kentucky, on Sunday, April 1, 1888, when a Black man accused of writing a note to a young woman was seized by the town marshal and threatened with lynching. He was released on condition that he leave and never return, and he left at once. The only known account is a short item in the local Semi-Weekly Interior Journal, which approved of the outcome.

According to the Interior Journal, Moran, whom it called "a negro", wrote a note "requesting a correspondence" with Miss Lizzie Shackleford, "a most worthy young lady", and left it where she would find it. The note asked that her answer be left in the same place; her race is not stated in the item.

Shackleford took the note to William Daugherty, who set a trap with Marshal Newland hidden near the drop place. When Moran came for the answer, Newland "brought his gun down and took him in". The paper said Daugherty was "with difficulty restrained from shooting" Moran, who begged for mercy.

Moran was then brought downtown, where "threats of lynching" frightened him so that he could hardly stand. A proposal to give him 1,000 [lashes] on his bare back was also made. In the end it was agreed that he could go if he left and never showed himself there again, and he left at once.
The item mentions no charge, court hearing or arrest of anyone who threatened Moran, and no later report of the case was found.

The Interior Journal ran the story on April 3 in its local column, between court news and a business notice. It told the story from the captors' side, calling Moran "the rascal" and "the scamp" and joking that he was told to "strike for tall timber". The item closed with a warning that if he were "ever caught here again he will repent his rashness."
No other white newspaper is known to have carried the story, and the Black press of the period is not available for comparison.

reader.title: Threatened lynching and banishment of Doe Moran
bases: The local paper says Moran, seized and brought downtown, faced 'threats of lynching' and a proposed whipping and was let go only on condition he leave and never return (A1); no one was killed or reported injured.

Moran was threatened with lynching and whipping and driven from town, but he was not killed (A1); the threat was extralegal and rested on his note to a young woman, but the number of people making it is not given.
Only the Stanford Semi-Weekly Interior Journal's local column reports the episode (A1); no other white or Black report was found.

accounts.label: Local paper (captors' side)
accounts.gist: The Stanford paper told the story from the captors' side, approving of the trap and the banishment and describing Moran's fear with mockery.

framing.detail: The item called Moran 'the rascal' and 'the scamp', made light of his terror and his flight ('strike for tall timber'), and closed with a warning against his return.

record_check.record: after a Black man, Doe Moran, left a note for a young white woman
record_check.dossier: The paper calls Moran 'a negro' but does not state Lizzie Shackleford's race; it calls her 'a most worthy young lady'.
William Daugherty and Marshal Newland captured him; the people who threatened lynching downtown are unnamed
A private citizen and the town marshal made the capture; unnamed persons downtown threatened lynching; no crowd size is given

info: Sunday before the April 3, 1888 issue (April 1, 1888, Easter Sunday by the same column)
Stanford, Kentucky (the paper's home town; Moran was 'brought down town')
Said to have written a note requesting a correspondence with Miss Lizzie Shackleford and left it where she would find it, asking that the answer be left in the same place
William Daugherty set a trap with Marshal Newland, who seized Moran at gunpoint; unnamed people downtown made threats of lynching; who proposed the whipping and who agreed to banish him is not stated
Released on condition he leave and never return; he left at once

sources.note: Only report: local column item on Moran's note, the trap, his seizure by Marshal Newland, threats of lynching and a whipping, and his release on condition he leave town for good.
quotes: SUNDAY a negro named Doe Moran wrote a note requesting a correspondence with Miss Lizzie Shackleford, a most worthy young lady, and stuck it where she was sure to find it.
Mr. Daugherty was so outraged that he was with difficulty restrained from shooting the scamp, who begged most pitcously for mercy.
He was brought down town and threats of lynching scared him so he could hardly stand on his feet.
If he is ever caught here again he will repent his rashness.
